nameStory: The Io moth gets its name from Greek mythology, where Io was a beautiful mortal woman who caught the eye of Zeus, the king of the gods. Just like the mythical Io who was known for her striking beauty, this moth is absolutely stunning with eye-catching colors and dramatic eyespots. It's also called the peacock moth for those same bold, colorful "eyes" on its wings that rival a peacock's plumage.
description: The Io moth is one of New England's most spectacular moths, belonging to the giant silk moth family. Males have bright yellow wings while females are larger with reddish-brown to purplish-brown wings, but both sexes sport huge, startling eyespots on their hindwings that look like owl eyes staring back at you. These moths are medium to large-sized with fuzzy, robust bodies and can have wingspans reaching 2.5 to 3.5 inches. Like other silk moths, adults don't have working mouthparts and live only to mate and lay eggs.

idTips.label: Hindwing Eyespots
idTips.description: Each hindwing has a large, perfectly round eyespot with a black center, blue ring, and white highlight that looks remarkably like a vertebrate eye - these are visible even when wings are folded and create a startling "face" when wings are spread

idTips.label: Sexual Dimorphism
idTips.description: Males are bright canary yellow with bushy, feathery antennae that feel soft and plume-like, while females are much larger with rich reddish-brown or purplish-brown coloring and thinner antennae

idTips.label: Wing Texture
idTips.description: Wings feel velvety and soft to the touch, with a slightly fuzzy appearance that gives them a rich, luxurious texture unlike the smooth wings of many other moths

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The body is thick and robust, covered in dense fur that matches the wing colors - yellow and brown striped in males, deep brown in females - and feels very soft and plush

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: When disturbed, they flash those eyespots suddenly by spreading their wings wide, creating a startling display that can make you jump - this defensive behavior is a key identification clue

idTips.label: Size Difference
idTips.description: Females are noticeably larger and heavier-bodied than males, with broader wings and a more substantial presence when encountered

habitat: Io moths are found throughout New England's mixed deciduous forests, woodland edges, parks, and suburban areas where their caterpillars' food plants grow. Look for them near oak, maple, cherry, willow, elm, and other hardwood trees, as well as around gardens with roses or other shrubs. They're attracted to lights at night and can show up at porch lights, especially in areas with nearby wooded habitat.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males often appearing first on warm evenings. This is when you're most likely to spot them at outdoor lights or see them during their brief mating flights.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season occurs through early to mid-summer, with adults most active on warm, humid nights. Caterpillars are feeding and growing during this time, covered in branching spines that deliver a painful sting.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may emerge in early fall in warmer years. Late in the season, look for cocoons attached to tree branches or shrubs as the larvae prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter in brown, papery cocoons that you might spot attached to bare tree branches or hidden among leaf litter and garden debris.

funFact: The Io moth caterpillars are living pin cushions - they're covered in branching, venomous spines that deliver a sting more painful than a bee sting, causing burning pain that can last for hours, yet the adults that emerge from these dangerous larvae are completely harmless and can't even eat!
confusionNotes: The distinctive eyespots make Io moths pretty unmistakable, but the yellow males might be confused with other yellow moths until you see those dramatic "eyes" on the hindwings. Remember: if it has eyespots that look like they're staring at you, it's an Io moth. The reddish-brown females could be mistaken for other large brown moths, but again, those perfect round eyespots are the dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "peacock moth" by some, this isn't related to the European peacock butterfly at all - the name just refers to the eyespot pattern. Many people are surprised to learn that these beautiful, harmless adult moths come from those notorious stinging caterpillars that gardeners learn to avoid.
compareHints: The Io moth is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other silk moths in the area like the Cecropia or Luna moths, the Io is smaller and has those unmistakable eyespots, while Cecropia moths are larger with red and white markings, and Luna moths are pale green with long tails. The eyespot feature really sets the Io moth apart from all other large moths in New England.
